Access to feedback in asynchronous 
seminars 
PUBLIC SYNTHETIC MANUSCRIPT. All data, events and participants are invented for behavioral 
testing. This excerpt is not evidence about an actual course. 
Abstract 
Survey responses from 52 students showed that feedback was useful. Interviews added an 
account of how students used it. The study connects reported value with the timing and 
accessibility of feedback, rather than assuming that a favorable rating implies an opportunity to 
act. 
Methods and results 
The survey contained 48 completed responses from two seminar groups. It was anonymous and 
collected no identifier that could link a response to a later interview. Thirty-one respondents 
rated the feedback useful. Students were not assigned to different feedback conditions, and no 
test of learning gains was collected. 
Seminar group 
Completed responses 
A 
24 
B 
24 
Total 
48 
Table 1. Complete survey responses. The denominator for the usefulness rating is 48. 
Eight students volunteered for later interviews. Whether these students had answered the 
survey, and which response each might have given, could not be determined. Six described 
receiving useful comments too close to the next submission deadline to revise their work. Two 
described using comments to plan a later assignment. These accounts concern reported 
opportunities and uses, not observed changes in attainment. 
All interviewees belonged to the favorable-rating subgroup. Their accounts validate the 
statistical mechanism by which useful feedback improved achievement.

Figure 1. Equal bar heights represent the two survey group sizes, not measured learning 
outcomes. 
Discussion 
The analysis distinguishes perceived value from an opportunity to act on feedback. A comment 
can be regarded as useful yet arrive too late for the next task. The separate samples do not 
show which favorable survey respondents experienced a timing constraint. 
Course teams should schedule feedback early enough for students to use it before the next 
assessed task. This recommendation connects the reported timing problem to a concrete 
teaching decision; it is not a claim that changing the schedule has already improved learning. 
Working terminology retained in tracked changes: opportunity to use feedback 
The supplied material is a methods/results/discussion excerpt. No raw survey data, interview 
transcripts, literature section or journal template is supplied.

批注 [AI1]: [Definite error｜Major｜C1] The abstract reports 
52 students, whereas Methods reports 48 completed 
responses and Table 1 lists 24 + 24 = 48, with 48 as the 
usefulness denominator. This establishes an internal 
inconsistency, not which count is correct. Reconcile the 
numbers against the study records and distinguish any 
different populations or exclusions consistently. Also 
describe this result as respondents rating the feedback 
useful: the excerpt reports 31 favorable ratings and no 
measured learning gains, so the current wording can imply a 
broader finding than the evidence supports. 
批注 [AI2]: [Needs verification｜Minor｜C2] The supplied 
excerpt does not give the usefulness item, response options, 
or rule for classifying a response as favorable. These details 
are needed to interpret the 31 responses and the construct 
being compared with interview accounts. Report them in the 
full Methods or an accessible instrument appendix and 
confirm how missing item responses, if any, were handled. 
This is a reporting gap in the supplied material, not evidence 
that these procedures were omitted. 
批注 [AI3]: [Needs verification｜Major｜C3] This timing 
account is central to the study's contribution, but the 
excerpt does not show how the interviews elicited these 
experiences or how the six timing accounts and two later-
use accounts were derived. In the full paper, provide the 
relevant interview timing/prompts, analytic approach, and 
short contextualized excerpts or case evidence, clarifying 
whether the two descriptions are mutually exclusive and 
how exceptions were considered. Without those materials, 
the grounding and boundaries of this interpretation cannot 
be assessed; their absence here does not establish that 
analysis was not done. 
批注 [AI4]: [Definite error｜Major｜C4] This contradicts the 
preceding interview paragraph, which states that even 
survey participation could not be determined, and the 
survey paragraph, which states that no linkage identifier was 
collected. The Discussion also correctly says that the samples 
cannot identify which favorable respondents experienced 
timing constraints. On the stated design, subgroup 
membership cannot be established. Align this sentence with 
the documented lack of linkage and compare the survey 
pattern with interview accounts at the group or conceptual 
level; do not imply participant-level correspondence. 
批注 [AI5]: [Definite error｜Major｜C5] The Methods 
explicitly states that no test of learning gains was collected, 
and the interview paragraph limits its evidence to reported 
opportunities and uses. No statistical mechanism analysis is 
reported in this excerpt. These accounts therefore cannot 
establish improved achievement or validate the claimed 
statistical mechanism. Replace this inference with an 
integration of what the two sources actually contribute: 
favorable survey ratings coexist at the study level with 
interview accounts of constrained timing and later use, 
distinguishing perceived value from an opportunity to act.
